articles.title: Fury vs Joshua: Heavyweights trade jokes at launch event
articles.summary: After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchange pleasantries, trade jokes and even discuss going for a pint at a news conference in London.
articles.body:
After more than a decade of public feuding and false starts, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua exchanged pleasantries, traded jokes and even discussed going for a pint at a news conference in London.

The British heavyweight rivals will fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

But for all the history between them, the launch felt more like two veterans in the closing stages of long, turbulent careers taking stock of how far they had both come.

"He's been a role model and poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury, 38, said of Joshua. "I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans in the street."

On Monday, there was still uncertainty over whether the fight would happen because of contractual disagreements surrounding the promotion.

There had been plenty of reason to expect fireworks on Wednesday. Instead, Joshua, 36, spoke about the magnitude of the event.

"It's breathtaking and I'm not saying that lightly," he said.

"I'm really grateful for this opportunity and bringing it to Great Britain because I know people in pubs have had proper fights about who will win and family members have fallen out."

The mood was perhaps best summed up at the face-off, when Joshua smiled and pretended to tickle Fury's stomach.

Relive Fury & Joshua's jovial news conference

Fury & Joshua in London for news conference as doubts ease

Common ground, catchphrases & old sparring stories

There was something almost surreal about seeing Fury and Joshua finally sitting side by side after so many years in which their rivalry had existed mostly through interviews, social media and failed negotiations.

Both had arrived hours earlier for one-to-one interviews. When the news conference began, master of ceremonies Michael Buffer introduced the pair as fireworks shot up from the front of the stage.

They entered from opposite sides at the same time - Joshua relaxed and composed in a grey tracksuit and sunglasses, Fury in more flamboyant fashion in a vivid emerald-green suit covered in crown motifs over a white shirt.

Alongside the world's media, a few hundred fans filled the balcony above and quickly made their allegiance known as "Oh Anthony Joshua" rang around the British Airways ARC.

Joshua has been credited with pushing to keep the fight in Britain and, if Wednesday was any indication, can expect strong backing in Cardiff - even with the main event potentially starting about 02:00 GMT to suit American audiences.

For two men whose names have been linked for so long, Fury and Joshua have spent remarkably little time together. But their famous sparring session in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur, soon became the topic of conversation.

Fury suggested he had got the better of it, prompting one fan to shout: "Liar." Joshua smiled and said he could not remember.

For those who believe the fight has come years too late, Fury had a simple response. "It's the icing on the cake of two great careers," he said. Moments later, he glanced back at the word "Finally" on the giant screen behind them.

There were several moments of common ground. Fury nodded along as Joshua spoke about his Christian faith and, even when the pair traded insults, they rarely felt venomous.

"This man here is carved in stone and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over," Fury said.

"When I crack him on the jaw with a big right hand, he's going down."

Joshua laughed and shouted back Fury's own catchphrase: "Get up."

The fight has been reported as being for the vacant WBA 'super' heavyweight title, although current WBA heavyweight champion Murat Gassiev's team has lodged a formal objection over the proposed title arrangement.

For a moment, it appeared the mood could turn when Joshua revealed he had received a call asking whether Fury's name could appear first in the promotion.

"You've been crying behind the scenes to get out of this fight. I've checkmated you. You have to fight," Fury replied.

"I've actually never won a world title here. Now it's on the line, we can become a three-time."

That exchange came after several chaotic days in which the role of UFC and Zuffa Boxing chief Dana White had threatened to overshadow the fight.

Netflix had presented White as part of the promotion alongside Turki Alalshikh's The Ring, despite Joshua promoter Eddie Hearn insisting his fighter's contract prevented White from having a promotional role.

But White did not attend Wednesday's launch. And when Alalshikh thanked the American from the stage, his name was met with jeers from sections of the crowd.

Fury did momentarily take aim at Hearn, calling him a "sausage" - but even that did not last long.

Within minutes, Fury was offering to go for a pint with the Matchroom boss - and extended the invitation to Joshua.

"I hope after this fight we can have a pint of Guinness together," Fury said. "Win, lose or draw, let's bury the hatchet."

"I don't know if I can trust you," Joshua replied, drawing laughter.

The overriding mood was one of relief between two veterans, who were seemingly happy to let the fight settle what years of talk could not.

articles.body: Ailin Perez has revealed a private Instagram message she says came from Norma Dumont after their UFC Vegas 121 fight, adding another chapter to their long-running feud. Perez showed the message during an appearance on The Ariel Helwani Show, where she said Dumont told her she would “hit” her again when they met. The message came after Perez beat Dumont by unanimous decision in the co-main event on September 26. All three judges scored the fight 29-28 for Perez. Dumont strongly disputed the result and later said she did not accept the decision.Ailin Perez shows Norma Dumont’s Instagram message after UFC Vegas 121Speaking through a translator, Perez explained why she shared the DM and said the rivalry between the two fighters had not ended with the final bell.“We don’t like each other,” Perez said through a translator. “We are not friends. We are never going to be friends. Funnily enough, after the fight, she actually wrote to me personally on Instagram, and she actually told me that after the fight, she was going to find me and beat the s*** out of me.“She’s looking for it right now. Here’s the message: ‘I have already hit you once, and I’m going to hit you once again when I see you. You already know that you didn’t win. Wink.’”The message refers to a previous incident between the two fighters, although the exact details of that alleged incident have not been independently established. Perez has previously said Dumont acted as if she wanted to attack her when they crossed paths at the UFC Performance Institute.“Every single time she sees me at the PI, she tries to look at me like she’s going to hit me,” Perez added. “Even when we were in the locker room, and we ran into each other while I was by myself, she would do things to make me think that she’s about to attack me, but she never does. But usually, she’s like that when she’s around her female friends, like the girls she has around her.”Perez also said Dumont had posted an angry message before their fight.“Before the fight, she posted a story, and Norma wrote in Portuguese, ‘F*** you,” Perez added further.Norma Dumont rejects Ailin Perez’s UFC Vegas 121 winThe tension was already high before the fight, and the result made it worse. Perez won despite Dumont landing more significant strikes overall. Fight statistics show Dumont landed 46 significant strikes to Perez’s 37, while both fighters had one takedown. Perez, however, had 3:41 of control time compared with Dumont’s 0:40.Dumont did not hide her anger after the scorecards were announced. In a statement posted on Instagram, she questioned the decision and said she believed she had won the second and third rounds.“Guys, the fight just ended, and for me, it was one of the biggest absurdities I’ve ever seen in MMA,” Dumont said in Portuguese on Instagram. “For me, the second round was clear, and in the third, the Argentine did nothing. She went to the hospital to get her head checked because of how f**ked up she is.”“She did nothing in the third round. Nothing, and she knows it. I was knocking her around and talking to her. I was hitting her and talking to her, and she was desperate. I was well aware that I won the second round without a shadow of a doubt. articles.title: 3 Hall of Famers, 10 fights, 109 rounds: The forgotten rivalry that defined an era of lightweight boxing
articles.summary: Titans of their era, Bob Montgomery, Beau Jack and Ike Williams repeatedly risked everything against one another in a three-way rivalry that came to embody a...
articles.body:
A few years ago, boxing was abuzz about a quartet of talented lightweights all primed and ready to face each other for years to come. The so-called "Four Princes" of Ryan Garcia, Gervonta Davis, Teofimo Lopez and Devin Haney were young and supposedly hungry to prove who was the dominant force at 135 pounds.

However, the foursome have only fought a paltry two bouts against each other thus far. Davis knocked out Garcia in seven rounds in April 2023, and Garcia beat Haney by majority decision the following year at super lightweight. Garcia's victory was later changed to a no-contest after Garcia tested positive for performance-enhancing drugs.

Since then, all four except for Davis have outgrown the lightweight division and are now competing 12 pounds heavier at welterweight. Yet despite being in the same division once more, this writer would be surprised if any of them end up sharing the ring again beyond what's already being discussed. There's simply too much politics and ego standing in the way.

As disappointing as that recent crop of lightweights has been, there was once a time when the division featured three future Hall of Famers who were willing to challenge each other more than once to prove who was superior.

Bob Montgomery, Beau Jack and Ike Williams.

Montgomery was born in 1919, in Sumter, South Carolina, and he followed his brother to Philadelphia as a 15-year-old. In the "City of Brotherly Love," Montgomery found work pulling clothes out of industrial-sized laundry machines. He also started boxing as an amateur at a gym known as "The Slaughterhouse," which tells you all you need to know about where "The Philadelphia Bobcat" first learned to ply his trade with gloved fists. When he later turned pro, Montgomery was managed by Joe Gramby, Philadelphia's most influential Black manager and a Pennsylvania Boxing Hall of Fame inductee.

Jack was born next, as Sidney Walker, in Waynesboro, Georgia in 1921. After his mom died when was a kid, Jack moved to Augusta to live with his grandmother, who gave him the name Beau Jack. As a young boy, Jack worked by shining shoes at the Augusta National Golf Club, home of the coveted Masters tournament. It was there that Jack competed in many "Battle Royales," where where he and other young Black boys were ruthlessly pitted against each other by white organizers, often blindfolded, until one remained standing.

However, something positive came out of that harrowing experience as it led him to pivot from shoeshiner to caddie at age 18, where he was noticed by club founder and golf legend Bobby Jones. It was Jones who helped rally the club's members to fund Jack's nascent boxing career.

Like Jack, Williams was born in Georgia, in the city of Brunswick in 1923. At the age of nine, his parents separated, and he moved with his mom to Trenton, New Jersey, where he first started fighting in the streets to defend his turf as a newsboy. The future "Trenton Tornado" began boxing as an amateur at a local gym under the tutelage of former fighter Jesse Goss. In addition to excelling at boxing, Williams was also a varsity athlete on the track and baseball teams at Trenton Central High School.

What united Montgomery, Jack, and Williams were their hardscrabble upbringings during the Depression. All three had to scrap, literally and figuratively, to support themselves and their families, and all three turned to boxing for greater earning potential.

To gain an appreciation for their in-ring styles, we can turn to renowned historian Bert Sugar. In his book titled "Boxing's Greatest Fighters , " Sugar rated Jack No. 52 out of 100.

"Barreling into his opponents like a pinwheel out of control, Beau would provide enough smoke behind the fire to suffocate his foes, causing them to suffer gentle and gradual erosion," described Sugar. "Looking like a marionette with one string broken, Beau flailed away from every conceivable angle, his low-held hands throwing a smorgasbord of punches, bolos, hooks, crosses, and just about everything else imaginable with either hand."

Not far behind Jack in Sugar's top 100 was Williams at No. 60, who, standing at 5-foot-9, was an exceptionally tall lightweight. He was a boxer-puncher equally capable of using his reach to stymie his opponents as he was to tear into them with violent combinations. Evidenced by his 61 career knockouts, he was more than willing to choose the latter approach.

"With well-defined moves worthy of some of the old-time greats," said Sugar, "Williams used his lightning left to run interference for one of the heaviest rights in lightweight history, leaving most of his opponents with the same difficulty in their search for defensible borders as ancient Rome."

Although Montgomery didn't crack Sugar's list, he too was an impressive specimen. The fifth edition of "The Boxing Register" states that Montgomery "won acclaim for his aggressive, take no prisoners approach. His intense boxing style led sportswriter Johnny Webster of the Philadelphia Inquirer to dub Montgomery the 'Bobcat' because of Montgomery's way of continually moving forward and pawing an opponent until he got them."

It was Montgomery who was the first to turn professional in 1938, followed by Jack in 1939, and Williams in 1940. When all was said and done, the world-class triumvirate fought 10 bouts between 1943 and 1955, five of which were for the lightweight title.

In doing so, they set the division ablaze with bravura performances that attracted huge crowds across the country.

1943: Bob Montgomery vs. Beau Jack I and II

The first fight among them was between Montgomery and Jack on May 21, 1943, at Madison Square Garden for the New York State Athletic Commission (NYSAC) title in front of more than 18,000 spectators. Jack had already become a mainstay at the Garden, eventually appearing in 21 main events in total, a arena record that still stands today, which is a testament to his exciting style that elated the fans for years.

According to the Times Tribune, Montgomery "took a terrible drubbing" and "lost the first round by a wide margin in the face of a flurry of uppercuts and the free-wheeling Beau Jack attack."

But Jack's early success was short lived, as Montgomery bounced back to win the next three rounds. According to the Buffalo News, Jack was ahead going into the seventh round of a "fiercely fought contest," but it was all Montgomery from that point on as he couldn't miss with his potent right hand.

Montgomery scored the fight's only knockdown in the 11th, courtesy of a "whistling right to the chin." Although Jack beat the count and made a desperate attempt to rally in the 12th and 15th rounds, he didn't have enough firepower to tame "The Philadelphia Bobcat's" unbridled ferocity.

By the end, both of Jack's eyes were badly swollen, and Montgomery had claimed the New York title. However, the public didn't yet espouse Montgomery as undisputed champion, because he had already lost three times to former champion Sammy Angott.

Angott held the title from 1941-42 before vacating it because of a broken hand that hadn't fully healed after surgery. But he only took a four-month sabbatical before he was back in the ring in March 1943. Since Angott was back in the mix when Montgomery beat Jack for the belt, it only made sense to see a fourth match between Angott and Montgomery for all the marbles.

However, before Angott could get involved, Montgomery and Jack squared off in a title rematch just seven months later, on Nov. 19, 1943, at the Garden where another 18,000 fans were "amazed by Beau Jack's unexpected display of fire and stamina," according to the United Press.

The main reason for Jack's success was because he adroitly executed the game plan of his new trainer, Larry Amadee.

"At Amadee's direction [Jack] stuck close to Montgomery," described the Des Moines Tribune. "He mixed willingly at close quarters, slugged it out with both fists when the referee parted them from a clinch and coasted when Amadee gave the word."

After 15 rounds, both judges and the referee scored it for Jack, which allowed him to join Lou Ambers as only the second lightweight in history to regain the title from his previous conqueror.

Despite the loss, Montgomery didn't offer any petty excuses. "I just couldn't get going," the former champion told the United Press.

Just a few weeks before Montgomery-Jack II, Angott had beaten Slugger White to become the National Boxing Association (NBA) champion, and he now wanted to unify the titles against Jack. However, Angott had to wait once more as Jack next fought Lulu Constantino on Jan. 7, 1944, less than two months after his title win, and claimed a split decision.

Meanwhile, Montgomery took on Williams on Jan. 25, 1944, at the Convention Hall in Philadelphia. Williams was riding a 34-fight unbeaten streak, but the 20-year-old was about to experience the repercussions of trespassing into the "Bobcat's" den unannounced.

Montgomery was especially motivated to battle Williams because he was seeking retribution for his friend and former coach, Johnny Hutchinson. Two months prior, Hutchinson "had been slammed into a fog by this same, leggy Williams," according to the Philadelphia Inquirer .

After the opening round, it was all Montgomery due to his dedication to digging his claws into Williams's body. The Inquirer reported that Montgomery's "endless stream of hooks, swings to the stomach and ribs did everything but pound the fight out of Ike by the sixth round. He fought on heart alone after that, and the speed of his long legs that often saved him."

It looked as though Williams would last the distance until Montgomery finally caught his quarry in the last round when he scored three knockdowns, the last of which came via a crushing right hand that knocked Williams out cold. It took "nearly 10 minutes of give-and-take with the commission physician before Ike could be elevated from the canvas, and practically carried from the ring."

1944: Bob Montgomery vs. Beau Jack III and IV

Just one month after becoming the first fighter to stop Williams, Montgomery was shockingly knocked out in 63 seconds by Al "Bummy" Davis, the fastest knockout at the Garden since it'd opened in 1925. Yet despite that unexpected setback, Montgomery was back at the "Mecca of Boxing" only two weeks later to take on rival Jack in their trilogy match for the NYSAC title.

Somehow, Montgomery showed no ill effects from the Davis loss as "the action was fast and furious all the way," according to the Edmonton Journal. After another 15 rounds, Montgomery won a split decision thanks to the rally he staged in the last two stanzas.

This time it was Jack's turn to be gracious in defeat, telling The Republican, "I thought I had a little the better of it, but after all, it's not for me to decide." The paper also reported that Jack's next fight would be against the aforementioned Davis, while Montgomery would finally take on Angott for the undisputed title.

But Montgomery didn't meet Angott next, because five days after Montgomery-Jack III, Angott lost his NBA title to Juan Zurita. That left Montgomery free to meet Jack for the final time on Aug. 4, 1944 at the Garden — their fourth fight over a 15-month span.

Unlike their previous three bouts, their last was scheduled for 10 rounds without the title at stake. For this bout, the gargantuan sum of $35,864,900 went to the U.S. Treasury Department to support the war effort, and a large contingent of veterans were in attendance.

In another close affair, Jack earned a majority decision that was "magnificently successful from all angles," according to the Los Angeles Evening Citizen News. It was Jack's "whistling hooks and bolo uppercuts that were generally more accurate."

With the Montgomery-Jack chapter of this three-way rivalry concluded at two wins apiece, it was Williams' turn to be involved in the remaining five bouts. And his next fight was a rematch with the "Bobcat" for the undisputed title.

1947: Ike Williams vs. Bob Montgomery II

In the three years after his first meeting with Montgomery, Williams won the NBA title by stopping Juan Zurita and made two defenses. Meanwhile, Montgomery was still the NYSAC champion.

On Aug. 4, 1947, in front of more than 30,000 spectators at Philadelphia's Municipal Stadium, "the two transplanted southerners had battled furiously, with Williams holding the edge due to his rapiers lefts," according to the Associated Press (AP).

The defining moment occurred in the sixth round, when Montgomery "straightened up from his usual crouch style of fighting," and Williams nailed him with a right cross. Montgomery went down, and although he beat the 10-count, Williams' ensuing onslaught knocked the "Bobcat" down a second time and tamed him for good.

In his dressing room after the fight, Williams broke it down. "I just beat him to the punch," he told the AP. "I saw he was getting ready to throw his right so I let mine go first."

"I straightened up and walked into it," Montgomery added.

This time it was Williams who scored the conclusive finish thanks to his explosive right hand, which he could crack like a whip on a steed. His money punch earned him inclusion in the pantheon of boxing's most concussive punchers pound-for-pound.

With Montgomery-Williams II in the books, it put an end to Montgomery's participation in this series, and left Williams and Jack to duke it out in the final four fights.

1948-55: Ike Williams vs. Beau Jack I, II, III and IV

After beating Montgomery in their rematch, Williams won nine consecutive fights, including one title defense. Meanwhile, Jack went 12-3-1 after his win over Montgomery in 1944, but with all of those bouts having been contested above the lightweight limit.

Yet because of Jack's respected reputation, he was granted a title shot against Williams on July 12, 1948, at Shibe Park in Philadelphia.

According to the Herald-News, "an estimated crowd of 13,000 saw Jack and Williams put on one of the most sensational championship brawls in years." Jack, despite being a heavy underdog, took the first three rounds because of his "bucking, bobbing, throwing punches from every angle."

Williams started to turn the tide in the fourth because of his vicious body attack. The United Press reported that, "Again and again, Ike ripped in with close-quarter hooks that seemingly would have broken the ribs of a mule."

In the sixth, it was a barrage of punches by the champion that left Jack out on his feet, tangled against the ropes in a neutral corner. With Jack clearly defenseless, Williams implored the referee to stop it. But when he didn't, Williams had no choice but to continue his flurry until the ref finally stepped in. It was a brutal display of power shots that knocked Jack's head all around its axis. Watch the highlight below if you're not faint of heart.

Williams and Jack ultimately fought three more times, once in 1951 and twice in 1955, but none were for the title.

In 1951, Williams beat Jack by split decision over 10 rounds, a result that was loudly booed by the crowd of more than 3,500. Then Williams-Jack III ended in a draw, while Williams stopped Jack in the ninth round of their final fight on Aug 12, 1955, in Augusta. Since Georgia was the birth state of both men, it was a fitting place to end this historic three-way rivalry.

Looking back at the lightweight trio's series of 10 memorable battles, it can be best summarized as competition at its finest. Of those 10 bouts, only three ended inside the distance, which led to 109 total rounds of furious, evenly-matched action.

If you judge them solely on their records against one another, Williams was superior, having gone 4-1-1, while Montgomery was second at 3-3, and Jack was 2-5-1.

However, far more important than their records was their willingness to repeatedly face each other despite knowing they would have to go through hell to achieve victory — and knowing that their brains and bodies would pay an exacting price.

Yet they consistently embraced that challenge anyway. And it was because of that shared desire to face the best competition, along with their tremendous skills, that allowed them to build Hall of Fame careers and forge unforgettable legacies.

That collective attitude is one that Garcia, Davis, Lopez and Haney need to start emulating immediately, and specifically toward each other, if they have any hope of creating lasting legacies like the heroes of lightweight's past.

articles.title: Bryan Danielson Returns to Wrestle at AEW's Tribute to Pac to Honor Benjamin Satterley
articles.summary: Bryan Danielson is set to return to the ring following a surprise announcement on Wednesday.
articles.body:
Bryan Danielson is set to return to the ring following a surprise announcement on Wednesday.

Danielson announced Wednesday that he'll return to wrestling at AEW's tribute to Pac, and he'll team up with the Death Riders to honor Benjamin Satterley.

Satterley, known in AEW as Pac, died at the age of 40 on Sunday, a day after competing against AEW National Champion Andrade El Ídolo in the opening match of Saturday's All Out pay-per-view. Satterley also competed in WWE as Neville, winning multiple championships across both companies.

Danielson, who competed in WWE for years before joining AEW in 2021, was a founding member of Blackpool Combat Club alongside Pac and Jon Moxley. The BCC eventually turned on Danielson and formed the Death Riders.

Danielson and Pac met in the ring in July 2024, when Danielson beat him in a singles match in the Owen Hart Foundation tournament semifinals.

Danielson came into the ring emotional on Wednesday, and Moxley seemingly wasn't happy to see him at first, but the two eventually made amends and hugged it out.

Though Danielson has been semi-retired for the last few years, he had no problem getting back into form after teaming up with the Death Riders.

Whether Danielson plans to make any other appearances remains to be seen, but it wouldn't be surprising if he made a one-match return to honor the late Satterly. Either way, it was a touching tribute to a wrestling icon.

articles.title: Tyson Fury vs Anthony Joshua: Rivals show respect at friendly first press conference - but how long will it last?
articles.summary: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally settle their rivalry in a British heavyweight blockbuster at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Friday December 11; Fury and Joshua both traded taunts at their first press conference in London; the British duo then shared a face-off
articles.body:
Perhaps because of the uncertainty that has continued to surround the fight since it was announced, there was something of a surreal atmosphere in west London until the two biggest names in British boxing finally appeared on stage shortly after 6pm.

The whole thing suddenly felt very real, with the audible excitement of the relatively small number of fans who had been able to buy tickets to watch from the arena's upper tier clearly appreciated by both fighters.

With the two-time world champions sat just a few feet apart, attention quickly turned to how they would interact after years of verbal sparring from a distance.

Joshua's measured persona made his approach easier to predict, but the wildcard was which version of Fury would show up.

After a lengthy introduction from master of ceremonies Max Kellerman, the American's questions about the fighters' sparring session - which took place in 2010, when Joshua was still an amateur - produced some light-hearted banter.

However, Joshua soon took control of the proceedings to pay tribute to several people in his life who had passed away, including Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele, who died in a car crash in Nigeria last December that Joshua survived.

Joshua requested a minute of silence which was impeccably observed by everyone in the arena, before applause at the end of it, which Fury warmly participated in.

Whether it had always been his intention or Joshua's words had influenced him, Fury then offered some extremely kind words about his rival.

"This man is a two-time heavyweight world champion, Olympic gold medallist, and he has been a role model and a poster boy for British boxing for years," Fury said.

"I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans I meet in the street. If you could achieve 10 per cent of what this man has achieved, you'd be doing well."

While there is little doubt tensions will rise and less friendly exchanges will follow between now and fight night, both fighters made it clear that there is a great deal of underlying respect between them, with no obvious personal malice.

That was further underlined when Fury invited Joshua to join him for a pint of Guinness in the pub after the fight, regardless of the result.

Joshua's humorous suspicion of the invitation, however, perhaps reflected his surprise at Fury's approach to the event. Was the master of mind games at it again?

Few are better qualified to analyse this event and everything around it than Britain's former undisputed heavyweight world champion Lennox Lewis, who was in attendance.

Lewis is adamant that once Fury and Joshua are deeper into their training camps, their exchanges will become less friendly.

"It's too early, at this time [for aggro]," Lewis said. "You need to be in training camp and not see people for a couple of weeks.

"To be training hard and thinking about each other. Then when they see each other, it will be different, because everyone will be touchy at that point."

Fury also showed just how quickly he can switch from friendly to confrontational when responding to a video released by Joshua and his promoter, Eddie Hearn, before the fight was finalised. The video positioned Joshua as a 'landlord' coming to collect his money.

Fury suggested that the fact his name appears first on all the promotional material for the event proves he is the A-side of the fight.

"In the build-up to this fight, Eddie [Hearn] and AJ were talking about landlords, being the boss, being the 'guvnor', the rent man and all that," Fury said.

"When I look behind me, I only see one don and that's Fury vs AJ. Now you've come to get the rent and I ain't f****** paying because I'm No 1.

"I don't make a big thing about all that but we're going to walk out seeing Tyson Fury versus his opponent Anthony Joshua - an old dosser who works for me."

With several details still to be decided - including which fighter will walk to the ring first and be left waiting for his opponent - the battle of egos is only likely to intensify.

While the result is ultimately all that will matter, it will be fascinating to see the receptions these two legends receive in the build-up to December 11 and right through to the opening bell.

If the first press conference was anything to go by, Fury and Joshua are set to receive a huge reception wherever they go between now and fight night.

After the huge cheers that greeted both fighters as they arrived on stage, Fury's fans broke into his "get up" catchphrase, with Joshua playfully joining in and repeating it back to them.

It was also notable that there was little of the hostility often directed at one fighter by the other's supporters. Instead, the focus was firmly on backing their respective heroes.

Joshua remained on stage for at least 30 minutes after the press conference had finished, signing autographs and posing for photos with fans.

After protracted negotiations had left the British public tired of waiting, this ultimately felt like a day of celebration for everything the pair have achieved in setting up one of the biggest fights in the sport's history.

The question now is: how long will the feel-good factor last?

articles.title: Anthony Joshua predicts first-round knockout against Tyson Fury amid hopes of producing 'spectacular' victory
articles.summary: Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will finally settle their rivalry in a British heavyweight blockbuster at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff on Friday December 11; Fury and Joshua both traded taunts at their first press conference in London; the British duo then shared a face-off
articles.body:
The pair came face to face on Wednesday in London for the first time since the long-awaited all-British clash was confirmed for December 11 in Cardiff.

The fight between the pair of two-time world champions, which has been a decade in the making, appeared to be in danger of falling through amid a dispute over where it would take place, with Joshua and his promoter Eddie Hearn pushing for it to be in the United Kingdom.

Asked what the fight means to him, Joshua told Sky Sports News : "It meant a lot to me because of the fans. Bringing it to the UK meant a lot to me for the fans.

"And for me personally, as much as it is just another fight because I don't like to make too much of it - it's just what we do - it would be amazing to get the victory in spectacular fashion."

Joshua revealed that he wasn't necessarily willing to walk away from the fight if his push to have it staged in the UK had failed.

He said: "I wanted to do everything I could to make it happen and part of that was it being in the UK and we got that so we're here, but I wasn't completely willing to walk away from it because it still needed to go ahead.

"You just listen to the cries and the conversation of those people who love boxing and love competition.

"People who wanted it to be in the UK would have still been happy that it happened, but I think getting it here is the cherry and icing and everything that needs to be on top of the cake."

Fury has been installed as an early favourite by bookmakers for the fight, with the fact Joshua has been floored in the opening round of two of his last three fights undoubtedly a factor.

Joshua admitted that he has "vulnerabilities" but insisted he is "hard to beat" and not considering retirement regardless of the outcome of the fight.

Asked where he feels like he's at as a boxer, Joshua replied: "Durable, hard to beat, can show vulnerabilities, but makes it exciting for the fans at home.

"There's more to come. The Anthony Joshua journey doesn't end here."

On his opponent, Joshua added: "He performs to the level he's at as well, if I'm honest.

"He's versatile, and he's a good little mover around in the ring."

And as for what he expects to happen in the ring on December 11, Joshua said: "A knockout, if I'm honest with you. Could be in the first round."

Asked whether that's his gameplan, Joshua added: "Yeah, it is."

articles.title: B/R Staff Predictions for UFC 332 Main Card
articles.summary: You are probably well aware of the reactions fight fans have had to this Saturday's UFC 332 card in Salt Lake City. People just aren't thrilled about it—and that's understandable.
articles.body:
You are probably well aware of the reactions fight fans have had to this Saturday's UFC 332 card in Salt Lake City. People just aren't thrilled about it—and that's understandable.

Compared to your typical numbered UFC card, it is very weak on paper. There's no debating it.

Then again, UFC 332 is going to air for free on CBS. That means it's closer to a Fight Night card than your typical numbered card, and when viewed through that lens, it's actually quite good. It's certainly a lot better than many of the recent cards at the UFC Apex in Las Vegas.

For starters, it will be topped by a title fight, as Brazil's Natalia Silva takes on China's Wang Cong for the vacant flyweight championship, with longtime champ Valentina Shevchenko forced to vacate the belt due to injury. That's a pretty good main event for a free card.

It will also feature a compelling co-headliner, as red-hot bantamweight contender Payton Talbott looks to lunge into title contention at the expense of former flyweight champ Deiveson Figueiredo.

Before that, we'll be treated to a fan-friendly lightweight contest between King Green and Esteban Ribovics, and the long-overdue UFC debut of former KSW and ONE star Roberto Soldic, who takes on fellow knockout artist Khaos Williams at middleweight.

The main card opener will see middleweight power-puncher Ateba Gautier look for the biggest win of his career at the expense of Roman Kopylov.

It may not be the most stacked card of the year—and it certainly falls way short of other numbered cards—but it should deliver some memorable and meaningful MMA action all the same.

Here's how the B/R combat sports squad sees it all going down in SLC.

Flyweight Title Fight: Natalia Silva vs. Wang Cong

Adam Kramer: Silva's path to a title fight has been impressive. While she hasn't finished a fighter since May 2023, five consecutive unanimous decisions over a largely stacked group of fighters carries plenty of weight.

Back-to-back wins over Rose Namajunas and Alexa Grasso, in particular, feel significant heading into this fight.

Wang Cong comes into this far less experienced although with a similar line of unanimous wins. Her lone loss came in November of 2024 to Gabriella Fernandes, and it came by submission.

That feels noteworthy as Silva is likely to close the distance, grapple and threaten submissions throughout. The very threat of Silva's variety of attacks could slow Wang down significantly.

Wang will try to maintain distance with kicks and movement; Silva will try to close that gap throughout.

While Silva doesn't land a finish, she threatens enough to get a decisive win and title.

Lyle Fitzsimmons: Silva, to these eyes, has all the pertinent check marks on her side.

She's younger by a few years and, though she has six non-victories in 26 fights against Wang's one in 11, it's undeniable that she's been in against a far higher level of competition.

Wins against the likes of Namajunas and Grasso don't come easy, but they're exactly what Silva has managed in the last 16 months.

Tom Taylor: Looks like we're unanimous on this one.

I'm totally sold on Silva. Her recent win over Namajunas was very impressive, and her preceding victory over Grasso—who has recently evolved into one of the most violent fighters in their division—has aged tremendously well.

Silva has a better resume than just about any other fighter in the weight class outside of outgoing champ Valentina Shevchenko, and she has the skills to dictate the terms of this fight with Wang.

She'll need to be careful on the feet with Wang, of course, but unless she walks right into a devastating shot, she should win this one handily with her grappling alone.

Bantamweight: Deiveson Figueiredo vs. Payton Talbott

Adam Kramer: This is the co-main event on a numbered card? Really?

Look, maybe it's a good fight. Maybe Figueiredo, who has lost four of his last five fights, finds his championship form once again. We've seen him do it, and he's done extraordinary things in the octagon over the past decade.

Still, he's 10 years older than Talbott, who is incredibly violent and capable. He's also recovered nicely after a loss to Raoni Barcelos, who we have seen fight incredibly well of late. That loss has only gotten better with age.

The question is whether this one goes to the judges or not. Unfortunately for Figueiredo, we don't believe it gets that far.

Lyle Fitzsimmons: I'm with anyone who asks how this could possibly be a co-main on a significant card.

Figueiredo will be remembered long after he peels off the gloves, thanks to a fan-friendly style and an epic flyweight rivalry with Brandon Moreno.

But his best days are behind him and his performances as a bantamweight have been, kindly, pedestrian. It's not pleasant for fans to see him fed to a rising 28-year-old here, but Talbott already sent Henry Cejudo packing so why not do it again?

Tom Taylor: I can see why my colleagues are disappointed this fight has landed in the co-headlining spot of a numbered card, but I'm also glad to see Talbott getting a big push from the UFC. He deserves it.

He's an incredibly talented and exciting fighter, and he's also a clear outlier in a sport that is marked by brainless machismo, virulent trash talk, and a relentless quest for viral moments at any cost. He seems like a thoughtful and genuinely good person, and those seem to be hard to find in combat sports these days.

All that to say, I'm backing him to dominate Figueiredo.

The Brazilian has an outstanding legacy, but at 38, he appears to be declining. Talbott's youth, pace and recent form could prove decisive if he is able to force a sustained, high-tempo fight.

Throw in the fact that the American is rangier, bigger and a lot younger, and I just don't really see how he can lose.

Prediction: Talbott by unanimous decision

Lightweight: King Green vs. Esteban Ribovics

Adam Kramer: Now, this is going to be fun. If you want to see two elite strikers punch each other repeatedly for (maybe) 15 minutes, this is the fight for you.

In terms of strategy, this is a doozy. King Green's boxing is electric, and Esteban Ribovics uses brilliant counters that could make this one ugly in a hurry.

For as clean as King's standup can be, he would be wise to make this one ugly with clinches and dirty boxing.

Heck, he might even want to wrestle and abandon the prospects of my initial take entirely. And that's the strategy we're going to go with.

If King chooses to keep this one exclusively upright, it probably won't go well. We believe he'll make it ugly enough to pull the upset.

Lyle Fitzsimmons: Unlike Cejudo and perhaps Figueiredo, Green isn't the retiring type.

Even at 40, he's still squaring off with youngsters and faring well as often as not, as evidenced by four straight wins—most recently a first-round blowout of Terrance McKinney.

Can he perform the same number on a guy like Ribovics, who's split his last four fights since the start of 2025? I'd be lying if I said I knew for sure. And I'll probably regret saying no.

Prediction: Ribovics by unanimous decision

Tom Taylor: It's been cool watching a veteran like Green cruise into his 40s on a four-fight win streak, particularly after a pair of stoppage losses to Mauricio Ruffy and Paddy Pimblett seemingly signalled the end of his time as relevant fighter.

Unfortunately, though, I don't see his momentum continuing beyond this weekend.

Ribovics is far from a world-beater, but it's pretty clear he can at least compete with all but the best lightweights in the sport. For all his accomplishments, I don't think Green is part of that group anymore.

There are certainly ways he can win this fight, but he'll be up against a younger fighter with serious skill, real firepower and an iron chin, so I just don't see it happening.

I expect some fun exchanges early on—and maybe a couple of big moments for Green—but at some point, he'll suffer the same fate as Edson Barboza, who Ribovics wiped out a little over a month ago.

Middleweight: Roberto Soldic vs. Khaos Williams

Adam Kramer: While we've ragged on the card some, this fight is plenty intriguing. The UFC debut of Roberto Soldic is worth watching. The former KSW star is a finishing machine, showcasing great hands and violent combinations.

And at just 31 years old, he's still positioned to be a potential UFC star.

Khaos Williams is capable of his own finishes, something he showcased in May. His issue has been consistency. He's finished two of his last four fights; he's also lost two of his last four.

The oddsmakers see Soldic as a solid favorite here, and it's hard to disagree. Also, if this one goes the distance, I will be stunned.

Lyle Fitzsimmons: I like Williams plenty. Come on, it's hard not to like a guy named Khaos. But he's far from a lock under the best of circumstances, and these aren't them.

People have been talking about Soldic for a reason, and he's been installed as a solid favorite for a reason, too.

Williams could end things in 30 seconds, or he could be outclassed and find himself finished at some point. I see the latter as far more likely.

Tom Taylor : I've been in the building for a couple of Soldic's fights, and I'm very happy he's finally joined the UFC roster. It feels quite overdue, but as Adam said, he's still just 31, so he's hopefully got plenty of time to show UFC fans who he is.

He is an absolutely vicious striker, capable of knocking opponents senseless with his hands, feet and knees at a moment's notice. While his 2023 knockout loss to Zebaztian Kadestam is a little concerning as he prepares to take on a powerhouse like Williams in his UFC debut, I just can't see him losing.

It's really this simple: In a fight between a highly refined striker with massive knockout power, and a relatively unpolished striker with massive knockout power, give me the guy with the technical edge. That's clearly Soldic here.

He'll dictate the rhythm of the dance, set some traps and eventually land a fight-ender.

Middleweight: Roman Kopylov vs. Ateba Gautier

Adam Kramer: In many respects, Ateba Gautier is a unicorn. His size and reach will make him look like a giant in this fight, although that will likely be the case in most of his fights at 185 pounds.

As for that reach, he'll have six inches on Roman Kopylov in this fight. It's an astonishing advantage, and it will allow him to dictate this fight in many respects.

Still, Kopylov is dangerous. He's also only been finished twice in 20 fights. He will make Gautier work, and he's only gone three rounds once in his young UFC career.

Kopylov avoids the finish, but Gautier leaves no doubt.

Prediction: Gautier by unanimous decision

Lyle Fitzsimmons: It's been a rough stretch for Kopylov since the start of 2024 as a four-fight win streak has suddenly become a 3-4 skid in which he's been finished once and beaten unanimously on the scorecards twice.

He won his last one and Gautier is by no means a lock, but the Cameroonian is 10 years younger, taller, longer and has won six straight in UFC-affiliated scenarios.

Kopylov is a step up but looks like a manageable one.

Tom Taylor: I have no trouble picking Gautier in this fight. Kopylov clearly represents the toughest test of the hulking Cameroonian's career so far, but it's hard to see where his advantages are in this matchup.

Like Gautier, he's a striker, but he'll be at a huge disadvantage in terms of size and power, and he is also less aggressive than his opponent.

I suppose there is a world where he can somehow tire Gautier out and win a decision over three rounds, but that seems like a long shot.

It's far more likely that Gautier just marches forward and beats him up until he drops.

articles.title: Fury y Joshua, de buen rollo: "Espero que después de la pelea podamos tomarnos juntos una pinta"
articles.standfirst: Los dos púgiles intercambian bromas durante la presentación de su esperado combate de diciembre en Cardiff
articles.summary: Los dos púgiles intercambian bromas durante la presentación de su esperado combate de diciembre en Cardiff
articles.body: Tyson Fury y Anthony Joshua intercambiaron sobre todo sonrisas y bromas amistosas cuando por fin subieron juntos al escenario para promocionar la pelea de peso pesado que los aficionados al boxeo han esperado durante una década. Los golpes llegarán más tarde, el 11 de diciembre en Cardiff, donde los dos ex bicampeones mundiales se enfrentarán por primera vez. Será, además, en suelo del Reino Unido. "Diez años gestándose", comentó Joshua durante una conferencia de prensa en Londres —la primera vez que ambos boxeadores se vieron las caras desde que se anunció la pelea la semana pasada. "Ya estamos aquí… tenía que ocurrir en algún momento y no hay mejor momento que ahora". La pelea se promociona como la más grande en la historia del boxeo británico. La única pregunta es si llega demasiado tarde para zanjar la disputa sobre quién es el mejor peleador. Fury tiene 38 años y ya ha salido del retiro en varias ocasiones. Joshua cumple 37 dentro de dos semanas y sus únicas peleas desde que perdió su combate por el título mundial de la FIB ante Daniel Dubois en 2024 fueron contra el youtuber Jake Paul y Kristian Prenga. "La gente dice: ¿es demasiado tarde?... demasiado tarde. Es la guinda del pastel", comentó Fury, intercalando una palabra malsonante. Ambos elogiaron a Turki Alalshikh, presidente de la Autoridad General de Espectáculo de Arabia Saudí y de la Federación Saudí de Boxeo, por haber logrado finalmente que la pelea se concretara. Alalshikh señaló que quería organizarla en el estadio de Wembley, en Londres, pero se decidió por Cardiff porque no pudo obtener permiso para que el emblemático recinto capitalino permaneciera abierto hasta las 2 de la mañana. "Al final, Gales cumplió. Y aun así es el Reino Unido", afirmó Alalshikh. La bolsa de la pelea no se ha anunciado, pero medios británicos la calculan en los 200 millones de dólares. "Les están pagando extremadamente bien", manifestó Frank Warren, el promotor del equipo de Fury. La conferencia de prensa estuvo llena en su mayoría de sonrisas y risas mientras ambos intercambiaban algunas pullas verbales sobre una famosa sesión de sparring de hace más de 10 años, cuando Joshua todavía era amateur. Fue Fury quien habló más, aunque en general tuvo cosas buenas que decir sobre su rival. "Ha sido un modelo a seguir y el emblema del boxeo británico durante años", indicó Fury. "Me encuentro defendiendo a mi archirrival ante aficionados que me cruzo en la calle. Dicho eso, obviamente estamos aquí para pelear, y pelearemos". "Sé que en los pubs la gente se ha peleado de verdad por quién va a ganar entre Tyson y yo", dijo Joshua. "Sé que familiares se han distanciado entre sí por quién va a ganar… Estoy feliz de estar aquí, peleando y cumpliendo mi destino antes de dejar este mundo". Fury también destacó los cuerpos y estilos enormemente contrastantes de ambos: "Estoy aquí hoy como el campeón mundial de peso pesado con la constitución más rara en la historia del deporte", reconoció. "Soy calvo, gordo, barbudo, feo, lento y pesado, todo lo anterior". En ese momento Joshua lo interrumpió: "Es verdad". Fury continuó: "Y tenemos a este tipo aquí. Está esculpido en piedra como un olímpico, de mármol. Pero cada vez que le pegan en la mandíbula, se cae". Hubo palabras menos amables para Eddie Hearn, el promotor del equipo de Joshua, y por un momento, Fury intentó avivar algo de animosidad burlándose de que su rival en el ring se hubiera referido a sí mismo como "el casero" durante la previa. "Ahora llegó el momento de cobrar el alquiler, y yo no voy a pagar. Porque yo soy el número 1", afirmó Fury. Los dos boxeadores también discutieron sobre por qué el nombre de Fury aparece primero en el material promocional del combate. Pero nunca parecieron cerca de llegar a lo físico cuando se encararon en el escenario, y Fury ya se está preparando para invitar a su rival a una cerveza después del combate. "No sé si eres de beber, pero espero que después de esta pelea podamos tomarnos juntos una pinta de Guinness", indicó. "Ganemos, perdamos o empatemos. Peleamos primero y luego nos tomamos una cerveza. ¿Qué te parece?". Joshua respondió: "No sé si puedo confiar en ti".

articles.title: Topuria regresa en un gran estado de forma a sus entrenamientos en Miami
articles.standfirst: 'El Matador' luce un gran físico en su vuelta al gimnasio tras su derrota ante Justin Gaethje
articles.summary: 'El Matador' luce un gran físico en su vuelta al gimnasio tras su derrota ante Justin Gaethje
articles.body: Ilia Topuria ha regresado a los entrenamientos en Miami por la puerta grande. Después de su derrota en el UFC Casa Blanca ante Justin Gaethje, 'El Matador' se tomó unas semanas para sanar tanto física como mentalmente. Sin embargo, cada vez salen más imágenes de él de vuelta en el gimnasio, luciendo un físico envidiable y con ganas de recuperar el cinturón de peso ligero. Desde el 14 de julio hasta inicios de septiembre, Topuria desapareció por completo del ojo público. Su primera derrota profesional fue un duro mazazo, y las lesiones sufridas en el combate ante Gaethje fueron motivo suficiente para tomarse un descanso. Sin embargo, a principios de mes Ilia volvió con una carta a su hijo Hugo y un posterior ensayo donde hacía un repaso de su vida y de su derrota. Desde ese momento sus apariciones se han vuelto cada vez más asiduas, y en el martes ya subió un mensaje a su Instagram acompañado de varias fotos entrenando. Además, hoy el 'BOXR Gym' ha subido una foto de Ilia entrenando junto a Matthew Attalla. "No puedes parar la grandeza. Cualquiera que no contase con él, no puede contar. Casa de campeones", escribió Attalla en el post donde se le veía abrazado a Ilia A pesar de que Ilia está de vuelta en el gimnasio, todavía habrá que esperar varios meses para verle de vuelta en el octágono. Aunque ya ha superado sus fracturas de pie, nariz y orbitales todavía es pronto para su regreso, ya que estos entrenamientos son una primera toma de contacto para volver al ritmo habitual poco a poco. Por tanto, hasta inicios de 2027 no se espera que 'El Matador' regrese para intentar vengar esa derrota. Además, su hermano Aleksandre peleará en el UFC Qatar el 21 de noviembre ante Santiago Luna, por lo que primero tendrá que enfocarse en ayudarle y luego ya se centrará en negociar con la UFC el rival idóneo para su regreso y la fecha que mejor les venga. Poco a poco todo vuelve a la normalidad, aunque habrá que ser pacientes e ir quemando etapas para que la vuelta de Ilia sea a lo grande cuando esté al 100%.

articles.title: Dana White reveals UFC’s involvement in Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight
articles.summary: Dana White addressed missing the first Fury vs. Joshua fight and what the UFC is doing for the event
articles.body:
Dana White is still involved in the Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua fight no matter how much Eddie Hearn might protest.

On Thursday, the UFC CEO responded to questions about why he wasn't in attendance for the first press conference to announce the highly anticipated heavyweight fight, which was held in London. While White was absent, his business partner and fellow Zuffa Boxing executive Nick Khan was there seated next to Saudi money man Turki Alalshikh.

While the actual promoters for the event — Eddie Hearn for Joshua and Frank Warren for Fury — shared the stage, White revealed that his team is definitely still involved in the fight and in a major way.

I had the Contender Series yesterday, I had to be here [in Utah] today," White said when asked why he didn't attend the Fury vs. Joshua press conference. "I fly a lot but that's a little bit of a rough trip.

"Not only am I promoting the fight, we're producing the fight. UFC is going to produce the show. I don't know how that's a PR disaster. I'm right."

Of course that news comes after Hearn took a victory lap declaring that he was always correct that White wouldn't actually be involved in the upcoming fight.

"These guys, Dana, etc just played it all wrong," Hearn said on Wednesday . "I'm not even going to sit here and slag it off because what's happened to them over the last seven days has been one of the greatest PR disasters in boxing. I don't even have to go in on them."

"Was I lying? Was I wrong? Am I not the promoter," White told MMA Fighting on Thursday. "Am I not producing the entire f*cking event? The answer is yes. I think that's the difference between me and Eddie is Eddie's trying to win some PR battle. Eddie likes to see himself in interviews. He likes to talk a lot and talking will get you in f*cking trouble."

The fight is set to air on Netflix on Dec. 11 from Cardiff in the United Kingdom and it appears White is definitely going to be involved if the UFC is producing the show.

The original press release from Netflix had White's name involved in the promotion and it looks like the streaming giant is going to count on the UFC's production team to put everything together for the event.

articles.title: Early retirement? Jon Anik doubts Gable Steveson reaches 10 UFC fights — ‘How do you regroup?’
articles.summary: How long will Gable Steveson stick around after suffering one of the most humiliating and biggest upsets in Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) history? Tha...
articles.body:
How long will Gable Steveson stick around after suffering one of the most humiliating and biggest upsets in Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC) history?

That is the question UFC play-by-play commentator Jon Anik is asking after Steveson was knocked unconscious by Sean Sharaf in just 12 seconds at UFC 331 last month inside Crypto.com Arena in Los Angeles, California.

Steveson entered the matchup as an astronomical -2000 betting favorite following his dominant UFC debut win over Elisha Ellison ( watch highlights ). Instead, the Olympic gold medalist ate the first clean left hand Sharaf threw and crashed face-first into the canvas, suffering his first professional mixed martial arts (MMA) loss.

Now, Anik wonders how the heavily hyped prospect will respond to a level of failure he has rarely experienced throughout his decorated athletic career.

"Gable is now having to deal with an experience that a lot of athletes on his level just haven't had to deal with," Anik told Submission Radio . "It's one thing if maybe he got knocked out late in this fight, and even with the Reinier de Ridder-Bo Nickal fight, it did go into a second round. This dude got flatlined and knocked out in 12 seconds. So, how do you regroup?

"I think he leans on everything mentally, physically and his God-given talent that has gotten him to this position," Anik continued. "I still believe if Gable Steveson gets to 10 UFC fights, he's going to realize a ton of success."

The biggest question, however, is whether Steveson will remain committed long enough to reach that point.

After watching Steveson destroy Ellison in his Octagon debut, Anik set the over-under for the former NCAA Division-I national champion's UFC career at just 10 appearances. Even before the Sharaf disaster, Anik was not convinced Steveson would reach that number.

"But after his UFC debut, which went well, I went on our podcast and said, 'Over-under 10 UFC fights for Gable,'" Anik said. "I'm not sure he actually gets to 10 fights. This is an appreciable setback. So, I'm as curious as anybody to see how he responds from this, but it's a big deal, and this is not the easiest thing from which to come back."

Steveson, 26, owns a 4-1 professional record and still possesses the elite wrestling pedigree and freakish athletic ability that made him one of UFC's most celebrated Heavyweight prospects. Nevertheless, those physical gifts cannot erase the image of Sharaf flattening him with the first punch he landed.

Steveson has already promised that the loss will not define him , writing that the setback will "catapult" him toward greatness.

Getting back inside the Octagon will be the first test. Making it to UFC fight No. 10 could be the much bigger one.
